quests.explanation: Like 'apply' to 'application,' verbs ending in '-y' change to '-i' before adding '-cation' to form the noun.
Words ending in '-ible' often come from Latin roots ending in '-ibilis,' while '-able' words are more often pure English — 'compatible' follows the Latin pattern.
This technical compound word measures how 'wide' a 'band' of frequencies is for transmitting data.
The prefix 'en-' means 'to put into a state,' so 'encryption' is the process of putting data 'into' a coded, secret form.
The prefix 'inter-' means 'between,' so an interface is literally the point 'between' a user and a machine where they interact.

quests.hint: Tricky spelling: AL-GO-RI-THM, ending in '-thm,' not '-rythm.'
quests.explanation: Named after the 9th-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi, 'algorithm' keeps an unusual ending that's easy to misspell as 'algorythm.'
This technology term describes a 'broad' (wide) 'band' of frequencies that allows fast data transmission.
The prefix 'sub-' means 'under,' and 'scription' relates to writing — historically, a subscription meant signing your name 'under' an agreement.
Just add '-ing' to the verb 'stream' (to flow continuously), describing how digital video and audio play without downloading first.
The prefix 'com-' means 'together,' so compression is literally the act of pressing data 'together' to make it smaller.
This entertainment term originally described a bomb powerful enough to destroy a city 'block,' later used for hugely successful films.
This compound word describes the 'track' (recorded path) of 'sound' that accompanies a film or show.

quests.hint: Tricky letters: CHORE-OG-RA-PHY, with 'ch' sounding like 'k.'
quests.explanation: Borrowed from Greek 'choreia' (dance) and 'graphein' (to write), this word literally means 'dance writing.'
The suffix '-ance' turns the verb 'perform' into a noun describing the act or quality of performing.
This compound word describes a 'piece' of work so skilled it could only be made by a true 'master.'
The root 'anim' relates to Latin for 'life' or 'spirit,' so animation literally means 'bringing to life' through drawn or digital images.
This compound word describes a 'play' written specifically for the 'screen' (film or television), unlike a stage play.
Related to 'spectator' and 'spectacle,' this word shares the root 'spect' (to look) — something spectacular is worth looking at.
The silent 'h' after 'ex' is easy to forget; this word relates to Latin 'hilaris' (cheerful), the same root as 'hilarious.'
The root 'captiv' relates to 'capture,' so something captivating 'captures' your attention completely.
The prefix 'co-' means 'together,' and 'laborate' relates to 'labor' (work) — to collaborate is literally to 'work together.'
This vivid compound word pictures ideas swirling like a 'storm' inside your 'brain' during creative thinking.
The suffix '-ive' turns the verb 'initiate' (to begin) into a noun or adjective describing the quality of starting things independently.
The suffix '-able' means 'capable of,' so being accountable means being capable of giving an 'account' or explanation for your actions.
When an adjective ends in '-ent,' the noun form usually changes to '-ency,' as in 'transparent' to 'transparency.'
The suffix '-ment' turns the verb 'accomplish' into a noun describing the achievement itself.
When a verb ends in silent 'e,' the noun form usually drops it before adding '-ance,' as in 'persevere' to 'perseverance.'
The suffix '-ful' means 'full of,' so someone resourceful is 'full of' resources, ideas, or solutions.
Related to Latin 'versare' (to turn), 'versatile' describes someone who can easily 'turn' to different tasks or skills.
The prefix 'in-' here means 'into,' and 'novate' relates to 'new' — to innovate is literally to bring something 'new' into existence.
